partialText:

title: Everyone Rushed to Deploy AI Agents. Now the Security Debt Is Coming Due
partialText:
Over the past two years, companies added AI agents fast and left security for later. Now many CTOs can't say how many agents they have or what those agents can access. The risk isn't only the AI model. It's everything around it: prompts, tools, data, APIs, passwords and keys, and third-party connections. The fix starts with a simple step: make a full list of every AI agent, who owns it, and what it can touch. Think of it as an AI agent bill of materials. From there, test agents for prompt injection, check where credentials are stored, limit access, review vendors, and make sure logs show what each agent did. Repeat these checks whenever something changes.

title: The Mathematics That Breaks the Biggest Myths About AI
partialText:
A lot of what we call AI limitations are actually geometry problems. More data, longer context windows, bigger models, and higher-dimensional embeddings are not always the right fix. Sometimes the model is being forced to learn the same structure again and again because that structure was never built into the mathematics in the first place. This article looks at five familiar assumptions about AI and attacks them with geometry, symmetry, topology, holonomy, hyperbolic space, and group theory. The basic idea is simple: if rotations, hierarchies, prompt order, memory, or other transformations have a mathematical structure, an AI system should not have to rediscover that structure from scratch every time. In short, better AI may not always come from making models bigger. In some cases, it may come from putting them in a better mathematical space.
